subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Rosy Retrospection
description: A micro-lesson that makes Rosy Retrospection usable.

hook.text: Your college years feel magical in memory. Your diary from that time tells a different story.

buildup.text: Mitchell found that vacationers rated trips more positively in memory than they did during the trip.

discovery.text: Rosy retrospection: we recall past events more favorably than we experienced them at the time.

twist.text: The brain edits out boredom, discomfort, and frustration. The highlight reel replaces the full film.

climax.text: Nostalgia isn't accurate. It's your brain's edited greatest-hits album of the past.

punchline.text: The good old days weren't that good.

quiz.question: What does rosy retrospection cause?
options: We recall past events more positively than they were
We remember the worst parts more vividly

details.summary: Rosy retrospection is the tendency to remember past events more positively than they were actually experienced. Vacations, relationships, and past jobs are recalled as better than they felt at the time, because negative details fade faster than positive ones.
details.whyItMatters: Rosy retrospection distorts learning from experience. If the past seems better than it was, people undervalue present improvements, resist necessary changes, and make poor comparisons between current options and idealized memories.
takeaways: Negative experiences fade from memory faster than positive ones
Past events are recalled as more enjoyable than real-time reports showed
Nostalgia-driven decisions are based on inaccurate emotional memories

faq.question: How do we know past events are remembered more positively?
faq.answer: Studies tracking real-time experience reports versus later memories show consistent positivity shifts. Vacationers rate their trips higher in memory than in daily diary entries during the trip. The negative moments are selectively forgotten.

faq.question: How does rosy retrospection affect decision-making?
faq.answer: It makes people repeat experiences that were not actually enjoyable, resist changes because the past seems better than it was, and reject current options in favor of returning to idealized previous situations that never quite existed as remembered.
